power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Survivin (BIRC5) is broadly overexpressed in human cancers but, as a self-antigen, is subject to immune tolerance that limits spontaneous antitumour immunity.

OVM-200 is a recombinant overlapping peptide vaccine spanning full-length survivin, with cathepsin S-cleavable linker sequences inserted between adjacent peptides to enhance antigen processing and presentation.
OVM-200-100 was a multicentre, open-label phase 1 study conducted at 4 UK sites.
The pooled 2,000-μg cohort comprised 27 patients with advanced non-small cell lung, ovarian or prostate cancer, including 24 patients from phase 1b and 3 treated at this dose in phase 1a.
OVM-200 was administered subcutaneously every 2 weeks for 3 initial vaccinations, with up to 8 additional doses in patients deriving clinical benefit.
The primary endpoint was safety and tolerability, secondary endpoints included survivin-specific immunogenicity, and antitumour activity by RECIST v1.1 was exploratory.
OVM-200-related adverse events were exclusively.
Therapeutic cancer vaccines aim to induce tumour-specific immune responses capable of controlling or eliminating established malignancies 1 .
text.formatted: Therapeutic cancer vaccines aim to induce tumour-specific immune responses capable of controlling or eliminating established malignancies <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> .

text.text: Recent clinical studies have demonstrated encouraging activity for personalised neoantigen vaccines, highlighting the potential of vaccination as an effective cancer immunotherapy [2] [3] [4] [5] .
text.formatted: Recent clinical studies have demonstrated encouraging activity for personalised neoantigen vaccines, highlighting the potential of vaccination as an effective cancer immunotherapy <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> .

text.text: However, personalised vaccines require tumour sequencing and individualised manufacturing, limiting their scalability, costeffectiveness, and timely delivery.
Consequently, there remains a substantial need for effective off-the-shelf cancer vaccines.
Most off-the-shelf cancer vaccines target tumour-associated antigens (TAAs), which are shared across patients and tumour types 6 .
text.formatted: Most off-the-shelf cancer vaccines target tumour-associated antigens (TAAs), which are shared across patients and tumour types <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: Unlike tumour-specific antigens (TSAs), however, TAAs are self-antigens and are therefore subject to central and peripheral immune tolerance, resulting in weak endogenous immune responses and limited clinical efficacy 7, 8 .
text.formatted: Unlike tumour-specific antigens (TSAs), however, TAAs are self-antigens and are therefore subject to central and peripheral immune tolerance, resulting in weak endogenous immune responses and limited clinical efficacy <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr">8</ref> .

text.text: Overcoming immune tolerance remains a major challenge in the development of TAA-based vaccines.

Survivin (baculoviral IAP repeat-containing protein 5 [BIRC5]) is a tumour-associated antigen (TAA) and multifunctional oncofetal protein that is overexpressed in a broad range of human malignancies but shows limited expression in most differentiated adult tissues.
It plays key roles in cell division, inhibition of apoptosis, and tumour progression, and its overexpression has been associated with treatment resistance and poor clinical outcomes [9] [10] [11] .
text.formatted: It plays key roles in cell division, inhibition of apoptosis, and tumour progression, and its overexpression has been associated with treatment resistance and poor clinical outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> .

text.text: These characteristics make survivin an attractive target for therapeutic cancer vaccination 12, 13 .
text.formatted: These characteristics make survivin an attractive target for therapeutic cancer vaccination <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13</ref> .

text.text: However, because survivin is a non-mutated self-antigen, endogenous immune responses against it are constrained by central and peripheral tolerance, which has limited the clinical efficacy of conventional survivin-targeted vaccines 14.
text.formatted: However, because survivin is a non-mutated self-antigen, endogenous immune responses against it are constrained by central and peripheral tolerance, which has limited the clinical efficacy of conventional survivin-targeted vaccines <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref>.

text.text: Previous survivin-based vaccines have demonstrated that survivin can be safely targeted and that survivin-specific immune responses can be induced in patients with cancer [15] [16] [17] .
text.formatted: Previous survivin-based vaccines have demonstrated that survivin can be safely targeted and that survivin-specific immune responses can be induced in patients with cancer <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[17]</ref> .

text.text: In particular, the survivin peptide-based vaccine SurVaxM has demonstrated favourable safety, immunogenicity and encouraging clinical activity in patients with recurrent malignant glioma 16.
text.formatted: In particular, the survivin peptide-based vaccine SurVaxM has demonstrated favourable safety, immunogenicity and encouraging clinical activity in patients with recurrent malignant glioma <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref>.

text.text: However, like many peptide-based survivin vaccines, SurVaxM targets a limited number of predefined epitopes and relies on presentation by selected HLA haplotypes, potentially restricting breadth of immune responses and limiting applicability across genetically diverse patient populations 16, 18, 19 .
text.formatted: However, like many peptide-based survivin vaccines, SurVaxM targets a limited number of predefined epitopes and relies on presentation by selected HLA haplotypes, potentially restricting breadth of immune responses and limiting applicability across genetically diverse patient populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16,</ref> <ref type="bibr">18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref> .

text.text: Vaccine platforms capable of presenting the full repertoire of survivin epitopes in an HLA-unrestricted manner may therefore broaden immune responses and extend the potential clinical benefit of survivin-targeted immunotherapy.
To overcome the limitations of conventional TAA-based and epitope-based peptide vaccines, we developed the recombinant overlapping peptide (ROP) antigen engineering platform.

Rather than selecting a limited number of predefined epitopes, the ROP platform re-engineers the full-length antigen, including survivin, into a series of overlapping peptides linked by cathepsin S-cleavable sequences, preserving the complete antigenic repertoire while optimising intracellular antigen processing and presentation 20 .
text.formatted: Rather than selecting a limited number of predefined epitopes, the ROP platform re-engineers the full-length antigen, including survivin, into a series of overlapping peptides linked by cathepsin S-cleavable sequences, preserving the complete antigenic repertoire while optimising intracellular antigen processing and presentation <ref type="bibr">20</ref> .

text.text: This design is intended to enhance the immunogenicity of self-antigens, broaden CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cell recognition in an HLA-unrestricted manner 21 .
text.formatted: This design is intended to enhance the immunogenicity of self-antigens, broaden CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cell recognition in an HLA-unrestricted manner <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21</ref> .

text.text: The disruption of the native three-dimensional structure abolishes the biological activity of the survivin oncoprotein while retaining its antigenicity, potentially improving the safety profile compared with administration of the native oncoprotein.
OVM-200 is the first therapeutic vaccine developed using the ROP antigen engineering platform and the first ROP vaccine to be administered to humans.
In the phase 1a doseescalation study, OVM-200 was administered subcutaneously at doses of 250, 500, 1000, and 2000 μg to patients with advanced solid cancers 22 .
text.formatted: In the phase 1a doseescalation study, OVM-200 was administered subcutaneously at doses of 250, 500, 1000, and 2000 μg to patients with advanced solid cancers <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22</ref> .

text.text: OVM-200 demonstrated a favourable safety profile across dose levels, with the 2000 μg dose inducing the strongest survivin-specific humoral and cellular immune responses.
Based on these findings, the 2000 μg dose was selected for further evaluation in the phase 1b expansion cohort.

Here, we report the results the pooled 2000 µg cohort of OVM-200-100 study, comprising patients treated at 2000 µg in phase 1a dose-escalation and the phase 1b expansion cohort, in patients with advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), ovarian cancer, and prostate cancer.

The objectives were to evaluate the safety and tolerability of OVM-200 at the selected dose, to characterise survivin-specific humoral and cellular immune responses, explore the potential association between vaccine-induced immunity and clinical outcome, and assess preliminary antitumour activity.

Between 15 Oct 2021 and 3 Dec 2025, 29 patients were screened for the phase 1b expansion cohort, of whom 5 patients failed screening, and 24 (83%) were assigned to receive OVM-200 at 2000 µg (Figure 1).
text.formatted: Between 15 Oct 2021 and 3 Dec 2025, 29 patients were screened for the phase 1b expansion cohort, of whom 5 patients failed screening, and 24 (83%) were assigned to receive OVM-200 at 2000 µg (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">1</ref>).

text.text: Three patients who had received OVM-200 at 2000 µg during phase 1a were included in the pooled 2000 µg analysis population, resulting in a total of 27 patients evaluated.

Of the 24 patients enrolled in phase 1b , 11 (46%) completed the trial and 13 (54%) discontinued: 4 died, 1 was lost to follow-up, 2 discontinued due to progressive disease, 2 withdrew consent, and 4 discontinued for other reasons.
Across the pooled 2000 µg cohort (n=27), 4 patients had NSCLC, 11 had ovarian cancer, and 12 had prostate cancer.
At screening, 26 patients (96%) had stage IV disease and 1 (4%) had stage III disease (Table 1).
text.formatted: At screening, 26 patients (96%) had stage IV disease and 1 (4%) had stage III disease (Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: The median age was 63.0 years (range 54-75), and 15 patients (56%) were female.
The most common sites of metastasis were bone [13 patients (48%)], lymph nodes [12 (44%)], liver [10 (37%)], lung [6 (22%)], and peritoneum [5 (19%)].
For the immunogenicity analysis, 26 patients were evaluable. 1 patient was excluded because evaluable samples were unavailable.

The numbers of patients contributing data declined at later timepoints: at week 8, antibody and T cell data were available for 23 and 22 patients, respectively; the corresponding numbers were 14 and 9 at week 16, and 9 and 8 at week 24.
For the assessment of antitumour activity, best overall response was available for 24 patients.
All 27 patients in the 2000 µg cohort were included in the safety analysis.
OVM-200-related adverse events occurred in all 27 patients (100%) and were grade 1-2 in all cases (Table 2).
text.formatted: OVM-200-related adverse events occurred in all 27 patients (100%) and were grade 1-2 in all cases (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: No OVM-200-related grade ≥ 3 adverse events, dose-limiting toxicities, serious adverse events, or deaths were reported.
One patient (1/27, 4%) discontinued OVM-200 because of an OVM-200-related injection-site reaction.

The most common OVM-200-related adverse events were injection-site reaction (17/27, 63%), injection-site erythema (6/27, 22%), fatigue (3/27, 11%), injection-site pruritus (3/27, 11%), and myalgia (3/27, 11%) (Table 2).
text.formatted: The most common OVM-200-related adverse events were injection-site reaction (17/27, 63%), injection-site erythema (6/27, 22%), fatigue (3/27, 11%), injection-site pruritus (3/27, 11%), and myalgia (3/27, 11%) (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

text.text: Other OVM-200-related adverse events included injectionsite pain (2/27, 7%), vomiting (2/27, 7%), and headache (2/27, 7%).
Grade 3 TEAEs occurred in 6 patients (22%), and none were considered related to OVM-200 (Supplementary Table 1).
text.formatted: Grade 3 TEAEs occurred in 6 patients (22%), and none were considered related to OVM-200 (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">1</ref>).

text.text: These events included vascular device infection, abdominal pain, dehydration, pneumonia, hypotension, gamma-glutamyltransferase increased, peritonitis, anaemia, nausea, vomiting, hypoalbuminaemia, ascites, and pelvic pain.
Serious TEAEs occurred in 5 of 27 patients (19%), corresponding to 9 events, none of which were considered related to OVM-200.
Overall, the safety profile was dominated by low-grade injection-site reactions and systemic symptoms, with no treatment-related serious toxicity observed.
Among patients in the 2000 µg cohort, 26 were evaluable for baseline antibody analysis.
The median baseline anti-survivin IgG titre was 20 (IQR 10-160) (Figure 2A).
text.formatted: The median baseline anti-survivin IgG titre was 20 (IQR 10-160) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">2A</ref>).

text.text: Following vaccination, median titres increased to 20,480 (IQR 10,240-81,920) at the first post-vaccination assessment (week 5-8), 163,840 (IQR 17,920-327,680) at week 16, and remained 163,840 (IQR 51,200-491,520) at week 24.
Anti-survivin antibody titres were higher than baseline at all postvaccination timepoints in every evaluable patient.
Across the cohort, the median peak antibody titre was 81,920 (IQR 17,920-327,680) (Figure 2B).
text.formatted: Across the cohort, the median peak antibody titre was 81,920 (IQR 17,920-327,680) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_5">2B</ref>).

text.text: OVM-200 also induced survivin-specific T cell responses, which peaked at the first postvaccination assessment with a subsequent decline over time (Figure 2C). 21 patients were evaluable for baseline T cell analysis.

In contrast to the durable antibody response, T cell responses showed an early expansion following vaccination, followed by a gradual contraction over time.
Across the evaluable cohort, the median peak T cell response was 505.0 SFU per 10⁶ PBMCs (IQR 176.7-734.3) (Figure 2D).

text.text: Together, these findings demonstrate that OVM-200 elicited both survivin-specific humoral and cellular immune responses in patients with advanced solid tumours, consistent with its intended mechanism of enhancing immunity against the self-antigen survivin.
A systematic search was conducted to identify studies evaluating spontaneous survivin-specific immunity in cancer patients.
Searches of PubMed (n=677), Web of Science (n=1,286), and Scopus (n=829) identified 2,792 records 23 (Supplementary Figure 1).

text.text: Following removal of 1,264 duplicates and five retracted publications, 1,523 records underwent title and abstract screening, of which 1,479 were excluded. 1 study was added during citation searching.
Full texts were sought for 45 studies. 4 were unavailable for retrieval, leaving 41 for eligibility assessment.
Studies evaluating spontaneous survivin-specific cellular or humoral immunity with solid tumors were initially eligible.
At full-text assessment, studies evaluating treatmentinduced responses (n=6), or without quantifiable measures of spontaneous survivin-specific immunity (n=1) were excluded.

Most cellular immune response studies, and some antibody studies, involved substantial in vitro antigen stimulation or lymphocyte expansion and were therefore not considered directly comparable measures of spontaneous ex vivo immunity.

As only 1 eligible ex vivo ELISPOT study remained, the quantitative analysis was restricted to spontaneous survivin-specific humoral immunity measured ex vivo by ELISA using titer/dilution-based antibody readouts comparable with the OVM-200 study. 12 studies were included in the final analysis.

To investigate whether OVM-200 could induce immune responses against survivin despite preexisting tumour expression of this self-antigen, a matched exploratory analysis was performed in 12 patients who had both pre-vaccination tumour tissue available for immunohistochemistry and evaluable immunogenicity data.

Immunohistochemical analysis demonstrated survivin expression in all 12 tumours before vaccination, including high (+++) expression in 6 patients, moderate (++) expression in 4 patients, and low (+) expression in 2 patients (Figure 3A), confirming widespread expression of the vaccine target antigen.

Taken together, these findings demonstrate that, although survivin was constitutively expressed in patients' tumours before vaccination, spontaneous survivin-specific humoral and cellular immunity remained minimal.

Vaccination with OVM-200 elicited robust survivin-specific antibody and T cell responses regardless of tumour survivin expression level, supporting its ability to overcome pre-existing functional immune tolerance to the self-antigen survivin.
Exploratory analyses suggested that repeated immunisation was associated with stronger vaccine-induced immune responses.
Patients were divided into two groups by the number of vaccinations: 1-3 vaccinations (n=11) and ≥4 vaccinations (n=12).

Anti-survivin antibody titres increased in both groups, rising from a median of 50 (IQR 10-160) to 15,360 (IQR 10,240-327,680) after 1-3 vaccinations (n=11), and from 25 (IQR 10-160) to 163,840 (IQR 81,920-327,680) after ≥4 vaccinations (n=12).
Patients receiving ≥4vaccinations achieved markedly higher peak antibody titres than those receiving only 1-3 vaccinations (Figure 4A).

In this combined dose-expansion analysis of OVM-200 at 2000 µg, comprising of 24 patients enrolled in the phase 1b and 3 patients treated at this dose in the phase 1a, OVM-200 showed a favourable safety profile and induced survivin-specific humoral and cellular immune responses in patients with advanced NSCLC, ovarian cancer, and prostate cancer.
Survivin is widely overexpressed in cancer but has limited expression in normal adult tissues 38, 39 .
text.formatted: Survivin is widely overexpressed in cancer but has limited expression in normal adult tissues <ref type="bibr">38,</ref> <ref type="bibr">39</ref> .

text.text: However, as a non-mutated self-antigen, it is subject to central and peripheral immune tolerance.

The induction of both antibody and T cell responses therefore provides clinical evidence that the recombinant overlapping peptide (ROP) platform can overcome functional immune tolerance and generate anti-survivin immunity in patients with advanced cancer.

Unlike conventional peptide vaccines, OVM-200 re-engineers the full-length survivin sequence into a recombinant overlapping peptide construct separated by cathepsin-sensitive linkers to facilitate antigen processing.
This design offers several potential advantages 20 .
First, the recombinant structure may increase immunological "foreignness" while preserving a broad repertoire of survivin epitopes.

Second, because the survivin sequence is fragmented by linker sequences, the recombinant protein is unlikely to retain the native tertiary structure or anti-apoptotic biological activity of survivin, reducing concerns associated with administration of an intact oncoprotein.
Third, processing of full-length antigen generates multiple peptides for presentation through both MHC class I and II pathways, supporting coordinated CD8⁺ cytotoxic and CD4⁺ helper T cell responses.
A further distinguishing feature is its antigenic breadth.

Earlier survivin vaccines commonly targeted selected HLA-restricted epitopes, including the HLA-A*24-restricted survivin-2B₈₀-₈₈ peptide 40 , while SurVaxM targets a defined 15-amino acid survivin region designed for presentation across multiple selected HLA backgrounds 41 .

text.text: By spanning the full survivin sequence, OVM-200 may enable broader CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T cell recognition without restriction to a predefined HLA haplotype.

OVM-200 was well tolerated, with toxicity predominantly comprising low-grade injection-site events and no dose-limiting toxicities, treatment-related serious adverse events, or treatmentrelated deaths.
This is consistent with the phase 1a study and previous survivin vaccine trials 16, 22 .

text.text: Repeated administration was feasible, with selected patients receiving up to 11 vaccinations without evidence of cumulative dose-limiting toxicity, supporting the feasibility of prolonged vaccination to establish and maintain immunity.
OVM-200 induced rapid and durable anti-survivin antibody responses, with greater numbers of vaccinations associated with stronger humoral responses.
Repeated antigen exposure may promote memory B cell and long-lived plasma cell responses, contributing to sustained antibody production 42, 43 .

text.text: In contrast, survivin-specific T cell responses were strongest at early post-vaccination timepoints and subsequently declined, potentially reflecting contraction of the effector response and transition towards memory populations 44, 45 .

text.text: Overall, prolonged vaccination appeared to have a greater effect on humoral than cellular immunity.

Humoral responses were also stronger in patients with stable disease, with anti-survivin antibody titres continuing to rise through week 24, whereas titres declined in patients with progressive disease.
A similar association between elevated anti-survivin antibody levels and clinical outcome has been reported with SurVaxM 17 .

In contrast, survivin-specific T cell responses did not significantly differ between stable and progressive disease, consistent with the SurVaxM study, in which T cell activation did not correlate with overall survival 17 .

However, comparisons with our findings should be interpreted with caution, because the SurVaxM study enrolled patients with newly diagnosed glioblastoma, whereas our cohort comprised patients with extensively treated advanced solid tumours.
The ability to generate broad immunity against a shared tumour-associated antigen provides a alternative strategy to personalised neoantigen vaccination.

Personalised vaccines, including mRNA-4157 (V940) 46 and autogene cevumeran 47 , have demonstrated encouraging clinical activity but require tumour sequencing, neoantigen prediction and individualised manufacturing.

text.text: In contrast, OVM-200 is an off-the-shelf vaccine that can be manufactured at scale and administered without patient-specific antigen selection.
It demonstrates that appropriate engineering of tumour-associated antigens can generate potent immunity despite pre-existing immune tolerance.
Several limitations should be considered.
The study had a small sample size and was nonrandomised, with a relatively short follow-up period.
In addition, the heavily pretreated population may have limited the ability of vaccine-induced immunity to translate into objective tumour responses.

Immune responses against survivin summarised in the systematic review should also be interpreted cautiously because of differences in tumour type, prior treatment and immunological assays used to determine antibody titres in different studies.
These findings nevertheless inform future clinical development.

The early peak in survivinspecific T cell responses suggests that additional immune support may be required to sustain effector function, and preclinical studies have shown that anti-4-1BB agonism can enhance the antitumour activity of survivin-based ROP vaccination 20 .
Potential combinations include costimulatory agonists, immune checkpoint blockade, T cell-engaging therapies and cytokinebased approaches.
In parallel, therapeutic cancer vaccine development has increasingly shifted towards earlier disease settings, particularly following surgery or other curative-intent treatment 46, 47 .
text.formatted: In parallel, therapeutic cancer vaccine development has increasingly shifted towards earlier disease settings, particularly following surgery or other curative-intent treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">46,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">47</ref> .

text.text: SurVaxM has similarly been evaluated into newly diagnosed glioblastoma following surgery and chemoradiotherapy.
In these settings, lower tumour burden and reduced tumour-associated immune suppression may favour vaccine-induced elimination of residual tumour cells.

These observations provide a strong scientific rationale for evaluating OVM-200 in earlier disease settings, such as the adjuvant and neoadjuvant settings, where induction of durable survivin-specific immunity may be better positioned to eliminate residual tumour cells and reduce the risk of recurrence.

In summary, OVM-200 at 2000 μg showed a favourable safety profile and induced survivinspecific humoral and cellular immune responses in patients with advanced solid tumours who had exhausted available standard therapies.
Together, these findings provide clinical proof-ofmechanism evidence for the ROP approach and support continued development of OVM-200.
OVM-200-100 was a first-in-human, multicentre, open-label, phase 1 study comprising a phase 1a dose-escalation followed by a phase 1b dose-expansion.

This study focuses on patients who received OVM-200 at 2000 μg, comprising those treated at 2000 μg during phase 1a (n=3) and the full phase 1b expansion cohort (n=24), for a combined 2000 μg analysis population of 27 patients.
The dose was selected on the basis of the phase 1a component of the study.

The phase 1b was designed to further assess the safety, tolerability, immunogenicity, and preliminary antitumour activity of OVM-200 in patients with advanced NSCLC, ovarian cancer, and prostate cancer.
The study was conducted at four sites in the UK.
Trial registration identifiers were ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05104515 and EudraCT 2021-001545-12.
Recruitment and follow-up took place between 15 Oct 2021 and 3 Dec 2025.

Eligible patients were aged 18-75 years and had histologically confirmed metastatic or locally advanced inoperable NSCLC, ovarian cancer, or prostate cancer, with at least one previous line of approved anticancer therapy.

Patients were required either to have exhausted recognised treatment options, to be in a planned treatment-free interval after a defined course of therapy, or, in the case of prostate cancer, to be clinically stable on anti-hormonal treatment.
Active anticancer therapy at enrolment was not permitted, apart from supportive treatment and androgendeprivation therapy for prostate cancer.
For NSCLC, at least one measurable lesion suitable for repeated radiological assessment was required.
Additional eligibility criteria included life expectancy of at least 3 months and adequate haematological, renal, and hepatic function.

Key exclusion criteria included clinically significant immunodeficiency; systemic corticosteroids exceeding prednisolone 10 mg/day equivalent or other immunosuppressive medication within 14 days before first dose; active or suspected autoimmune disease requiring systemic therapy; prior anticancer vaccine therapy, immune checkpoint antibody or T cell costimulation therapy within 28 days before first dose; investigational treatment within 28 days or 6 half-lives, whichever was longer; major surgery, chemotherapy, or radiotherapy within 28 days before first dose; active infection or viral disease; any vaccine within 28 days before first dose; symptomatic brain metastases or leptomeningeal disease; uncontrolled medical disorders; or known hypersensitivity to any component of OVM-200 or the adjuvant.
Survivin expression was not an entry criterion and was assessed only in a subset of patients as an exploratory biomarker.
The study protocol was approved by the South Central-Oxford A Research Ethics Committee

The primary endpoint was the safety and tolerability of OVM-200 at 2000 μg, assessed by the occurrence, severity, and relationship of adverse events, including dose-limiting toxicities, serious adverse events, and adverse events leading to treatment discontinuation.

Exploratory endpoints included associations between immunogenicity and clinical outcome; preliminary antitumour activity, assessed by best overall response according to RECIST version 1.1; progression-free survival; associations between survivin expression in tumour and survivin-specific immunogenicity; and durability of vaccine-induced immune responses.
The safety analysis comprised all patients who received at least one dose of OVM-200 (n=27).
Immunogenicity and antitumour activity were assessed in evaluable patients with available data for the relevant endpoint.

text.text: Radiological assessments were available for 18 patients at week 8, 6 at week 16, and 8 at week 24.
Patients achieving disease stablisation developed stronger humoral immune responses than those with progressive disease.

In the stable disease group, median anti-survivin antibody titres increased from 15 (IQR 10-55) at baseline to 30,720 (IQR 16,640-102,400) at the early postvaccination assessment (week 5-8), 327,680 (IQR 87,040-491,520) at week 16, and 368,640 (IQR 35,840-655,360) at week 24 (Figure 6A).

In contrast, patients with progressive disease showed lower antibody titres throughout follow-up, increasing from baseline, 60 (IQR 10-160), to 20,480 (IQR 10,240-81,920) at the early post-vaccination assessment, 163,840 (IQR 15,360-245,760) at week 16, and 163,840 (IQR 46,080-245,760) at week 24.

Overall, patients with stable disease developed significantly higher anti-survivin antibody titres than those with progressive disease (p=0.0418), Survivin-specific T cell responses also increased following vaccination in both groups (Figure 6B).

In patients with stable disease, median ELISpot responses increased from 43.6 (IQR 15.7-71.3) SFU per 10⁶ PBMCs at baseline to 712.5 (IQR 495.3-796.1) at the early post-vaccination assessment, whereas the corresponding increase in patients with progressive disease was from 11.4 (IQR 1.0-90.3) to 301.7 (IQR 122.8-714.1) SFU per 10⁶ PBMCs.
Responses remained above baseline at later time points in both groups.
Anti-survivin antibody titre increased from 10 at baseline to 5120 at the early post-vaccination assessment (Week 5-8), reaching 655,360 at both Week 16 and Week 24.
Survivin-specific T cell response increased from 17.4 SFU per 10⁶ PBMCs at baseline to 993.6 SFU per 10 6 PBMCs at Week 8 and remained at 547.7 SFU per 10 6 PBMCs at Week 24.
The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, Good Clinical Practice guidelines, and UK clinical trial regulations.
All participants provided written informed consent.
Procedures OVM-200 is a recombinant overlapping peptide vaccine spanning the full-length survivin sequence and formulated with Montanide ISA 51 VG.
Vaccine material was manufactured under Good Manufacturing Practice conditions by Eurofins CDMO (Ghent, Belgium).
The final product was supplied as a 2 mg/mL solution and emulsified 1:1 with Montanide before subcutaneous administration.
All patients received OVM-200 2000 μg subcutaneously every 2 weeks for an initial series of three vaccinations.
Patients were observed for at least 4 h after each administration.
Patients considered by the investigator to be deriving benefit could continue treatment for up to eight additional immunisations, to a maximum of 11 doses.

Baseline assessments were performed before the first vaccination, with on-treatment evaluation through the end-of-treatment visit at week 5 (day 36), and follow-up assessments at week 8 (day 57), week 16 (day 113), and end of study at week 24 (day 169).
Blood for immunogenicity analyses was collected at baseline (day 1), week 5 (day 36), week 8 (day 57), week 16 (day 113), and week 24 (day 169).
Serum anti-survivin IgG responses were measured by ELISA, with titres reported in two-fold dilutions starting at 1:20.
Titres below 1:20 were assigned a value of 10 (half the lower limit of quantification) for geometric mean calculations.
Survivin-specific cellular responses were assessed by interferon-γ ELISpot using peripheral blood mononuclear cells isolated from whole blood within 24 h of collection.
Tumour assessments were performed during study follow-up according to RECIST version 1.1, with week 8 and later assessments contributing to best overall response.
Safety assessments included adverse-event monitoring, physical examination, ECOG performance status, vital signs, laboratory testing, urinalysis, and electrocardiograms.
Adverse events were graded according to CTCAE version 5.0.
